chunks: Ahmad ibn Ziyad ibn Ja'far al-Hamadani - may God be pleased with him - narrated that Ali ibn Ibrahim ibn Hashim narrated from Yasir the servant, who said: Some of the chiefs asked Abul Hasan al-Rida (peace be upon him) about eating mud, saying that some of his female servants eat mud. He became angry and then said:
"Eating mud is forbidden, like the dead flesh, blood, and pork. Admonish them to stop doing that."

He said: And Yasir narrated to me that when al-Rida (peace be upon him) returned on Friday from the mosque, having been covered in sweat and dust, he would raise his hands and say: 'O God, if my relief from what I am in is through death, then hasten it to the hour.' He remained sorrowful and distressed until he was taken (peace be upon him).

Yasir said: A letter was written from Nishapur to al-Ma'mun stating that a Magus had willed at his death a considerable amount of wealth to be distributed among the poor and needy, and the judge of Nishapur had distributed it among the poor Muslims. Al-Ma'mun asked al-Rida (peace be upon him): 'O my Master, what do you say about that?' Al-Rida (peace be upon him) said: 'The Magi do not give charity to the poor Muslims. Write to him that he should take an equivalent amount from the charity of the Muslims and give it in charity to the poor Magi;'
And Ali ibn Ibrahim ibn Hashim said: And Yasir and others narrated to me many traditions from al-Rida (peace be upon him) which I did not mention because I heard them a long time ago.
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on eating mud in Shia jurisprudence and how is the charity of non-Muslims handled?
ai.summary: This narration from *Uyun Akhbar al-Rida* highlights Imam al-Rida’s (AS) juristic precision in distinguishing between *makruh* and *haram* by equating mud consumption with major impurities like blood and pork. It also illustrates the concept of *kaffarah* (expiation) in inheritance law, where the Imam ensures equitable distribution by balancing the Magus's bequest with equivalent Muslim charity, reflecting the principle of reciprocal justice. Furthermore, the description of his perpetual sorrow (*ghamm*) and supplication for death underscores the theological concept of the Imams' unique burden of leadership and their longing for reunion with Allah.

en.dr-ali-peiravi: 30-34 Ahmad ibn Ziyad ibn Ja’far al-Hamadani - may God be pleased with him - narrated that Ali ibn Ibrahim ibn Hashem quoted on the authority of his father, on the authority of Yasir - the servant, “One of the chiefs of the army asked Abul Hassan Al-Ridha (s) about eating mud. He said that some of his servants eat mud. The Imam (s) got really upset and said, ‘
It is forbidden to eat mud, just as it is to eat dead flesh, blood, and pork. Admonish them not to eat mud.’”

Ali ibn Ibrahim said, “Yasir narrated that once on a Friday when Al-Ridha (s) was returning from the mosque, he (s) raised up his hands to the heavens and said, “O my God! If my release from this bond is only possible by my death, please expedite it.” The Imam (s) lived sadly until he (s) perished.

Yasir said, “They wrote a letter to Al-Ma’mun from Neishaboor stating that a Magus had died and willed that a portion of his wealth be given to the poor and the needy, and the judge in Neishaboor had divided it up among the poor Muslim people as charity. Al-Ma’mun asked Al-Ridha (s), “O my Master! What do you think about this?” Al-Ridha (s) said, “A Magus would not give any charity to the poor Muslims. Write a letter to the judge ordering him to take as much money from the state treasury as he had taken from the inheritance of the Magi and given in charity to the poor Muslims. Then he should give that money to poor Magi in the form of charity.”
Ali ibn Ibrahim added, “Yasir and others have narrated a lot of traditions on the authority of Al-Ridha (s), but I have forgotten most of them since a great deal of time has passed by.”
